slides.title: Fenchel's Duality Theorem
slides.notes: Open by naming the section's change of viewpoint. Earlier duality material gave conjugates, support functions, and adjoint programs. This lecture uses those pieces to make one value equality visible: a primal minimum and a dual maximum agree once the domains meet in the right relative-interior sense.

slides.title: Two Ledgers
slides.notes: Rockafellar writes the theorem with a convex function f and a concave function g, so the primal object is f minus g. Translate this carefully for students who expect f plus phi notation: choosing g as minus a convex penalty or indicator recovers the familiar sum form.

slides.title: Weak Duality
slides.notes: Spend time on the inequality chain because it is the whole proof skeleton. Fenchel's inequality for f gives the pairing below f plus f star, while the concave version for g places the same pairing above g plus g star. Subtracting produces a nonnegative gap.

slides.title: Qualification
slides.notes: The theorem is not only an equality statement; it also says where an optimizer is guaranteed to appear. A primal relative-interior overlap gives dual attainment, while a dual relative-interior overlap, together with closedness, gives primal attainment. Polyhedral data reduce the need for relative interiors.

slides.title: Separation Proof
slides.notes: Describe the proof as a geometric certificate extraction. The epigraph of f and a shifted hypograph of g cannot cross at the optimal shift. The relative-interior condition rules out a vertical separator, so the separator is the graph of an affine function whose slope becomes the dual optimizer.

slides.title: Linear Perturbation
slides.notes: Now move from the identity case to the linear map A. The perturbation u translates the argument of g, so the value p of u records how the primal optimum changes under a right-hand-side shift. The adjoint A star is the bookkeeping device that moves dual slopes back to x-space.

slides.title: Perturbation Reading
slides.notes: Use the graph of p near the origin as the operational meaning of the dual variable. A dual vector is a supporting slope for the value function at zero. A jump or missing support at zero is the visual version of a duality gap or a failed attainment statement.

slides.title: Kuhn-Tucker Conditions
slides.notes: State the conditions as matched equality cases in Fenchel's inequality. The relation A star u star belongs to the subdifferential of f at x, and Ax belongs to the subdifferential of g star at u star. Together they certify both primal and dual optimality, not merely stationarity.

slides.title: Quadratic Indicator Audit
slides.notes: This is the notebook's finite check in a concrete one-dimensional form. The unconstrained quadratic would minimize at minus one, but the indicator half-line forces the boundary point x equals zero. The dual parabola peaks at p equals one, and both ledgers return the same value one half.

slides.title: Cone Consequence
slides.notes: The cone corollary should feel like a specialization, not a new theorem from nowhere. Replacing g by a negative indicator of a cone turns the dual variable into a member of the negative polar cone. Equality is then the familiar complementarity picture: primal feasible, dual feasible, orthogonal contact, and subgradient support.

slides.title: Moreau Decomposition
slides.notes: Moreau's theorem is the section's geometric payoff. Adding the quadratic w makes the two infima finite and uniquely attained, so every vector z splits into x plus x star with x star in the subdifferential of f at x. For an indicator function this is nearest-point projection and polar residual.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close by asking students to audit any Fenchel duality claim in four passes: identify the primal and dual ledgers, check the relative-interior qualification, find the Fenchel equality certificate, and test the perturbation value near the origin. That sequence catches most sign errors and missing hypotheses.
